solution.concept_anchor: Density and pressure increases with depth; geothermal gradient non-linear

statement_analysis.statement: Density of Earth's material increases progressively with depth, from approximately 2.7 g/cm³ in continental crust to approximately 13 g/cm³ in the inner core.
statement_analysis.reason: Density increases with depth due to both compositional changes (lighter silicates → denser iron-nickel) and compressional effects of increasing pressure. The values ~2.7 g/cm³ for continental crust and ~10–13 g/cm³ for the core are standard.

statement_analysis.statement: Pressure increases continuously with depth throughout Earth's interior and is measured in GPa at the level of the core.
statement_analysis.reason: Pressure is a function of the weight of overlying material (lithostatic pressure) and increases monotonically with depth. Core pressures reach ~330–360 GPa — validly expressed in gigapascals.

statement_analysis.statement: The geothermal gradient of approximately 30°C per km applies uniformly from the surface to the centre of Earth.
statement_analysis.reason: The ~30°C per km gradient applies only to the crust; the gradient decreases substantially in the mantle and core, where heat conduction mechanisms differ. Applying it uniformly would give absurdly high temperatures (>180,000°C at the core) — far exceeding the actual ~5,000–6,000°C.

statement_analysis.statement: Despite the inner core being the hottest region of Earth, it remains solid due to the extreme confining pressure that elevates the melting point of its iron-nickel composition.
statement_analysis.reason: Pressure at the inner core (~330–360 GPa) raises the melting point of iron-nickel above the ambient temperature (~5,000–6,000°C), maintaining it in solid state despite being the hottest region.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is the distractor; students who accept Statement 3 (the uniform 30°C/km gradient sounds 'technically correct' since it is a real figure) will count all four as correct and choose 'All four.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 3 — 'approximately 30°C per km applies uniformly from surface to centre' is clearly a scope-extension error; 30°C/km is valid only for the crust; the gradient decreases with depth; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 1 — density increasing from ~2.7 to ~13 g/cm³ across Earth's layers is a standard fact; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — pressure increasing continuously to GPa range at the core is correct; Statement 2 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 4 — inner core solidity due to pressure-elevated melting point despite high temperature is the correct mechanism; Statement 4 is correct. Three of four are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the scope-extension trap using the real geothermal gradient figure of ~30°C/km. Students who have memorised this figure without knowing its limitation (it applies only to the crust) will accept Statement 3 as universally true. Applying 30°C/km uniformly to Earth's ~6,371 km depth would yield ~191,000°C at the centre — clearly impossible given the actual ~6,000°C estimate. The restriction of this gradient to the crust is a critical qualification that distinguishes precise from superficial knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Earth's thermal, pressure and density profiles are non-uniform and each requires careful qualification.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Density increases from ~2.7 g/cm³ (continental crust/SIAL) through ~3.0 g/cm³ (SIMA), ~3.3–5.6 g/cm³ (mantle) to ~10–13 g/cm³ (NIFE core). Both composition and pressure contribute.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Lithostatic pressure increases continuously. Surface pressure ~0.1 MPa; Moho ~1 GPa; core-mantle boundary ~136 GPa; inner core ~330–360 GPa.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The ~30°C/km geothermal gradient applies only in the crust. In the mantle, the gradient drops to ~0.3–1°C/km due to convective heat transfer being more efficient than conduction. Uniform application would give impossibly high core temperatures.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The inner core is Earth's hottest region yet remains solid — pressure-driven solidification via elevated melting point is the mechanism.

Value Addition:
• Earth's mean surface heat flow is ~87 milliwatts per square metre — higher in volcanic regions.
• The mantle geotherm (temperature-depth curve) tracks the intersection between actual temperature and melting point curves to identify partial melt zones.
• Pressure at Earth's centre (~360 GPa) is about 3.6 million times standard atmospheric pressure.

solution.concept_anchor: Moho depth greatest under mountains due to isostasy
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) tempts students who correctly identify both A and R as true but question whether the causal relationship is reversed — they may wonder if Moho depth causes mountain height rather than mountain height causing deeper Moho.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Moho is deepest under young fold mountains like the Himalayas (~70 km) — an established seismological fact.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Isostasy (Airy's model) requires that thicker, taller crustal blocks must have deeper roots to maintain gravitational equilibrium — mountains float on the mantle like icebergs in water.

Step 3: Does R causally or logically explain A? — Yes. The isostatic requirement for crustal equilibrium directly causes the Moho to be deeper under mountains — the greater crustal mass above requires a deeper root below the Moho. R is both factually correct and causally explains A.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap tempts students to select option (b) by making them question the direction of causation: does a deeper Moho cause mountains to be higher, or does the mountain height cause the deeper Moho? In Airy's isostatic model, it is simultaneous — the two are in equilibrium. However, from a geophysical causation perspective, the crustal load (mountain mass) is the cause, and the depth of the Moho (crustal root depth) is the isostatic response. R correctly explains A: isostasy (the principle) causes the Moho to deepen under elevated terrain.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Moho depth and surface topography is a direct consequence of isostasy — one of the most elegant principles in geomorphology.

Assertion (A) is correct: The Moho is shallowest under ocean floors (~5–10 km) and deepest under young fold mountains (~70 km under the Himalayas). This inverse relationship between surface elevation and Moho depth is a well-established seismological observation.

Reason (R) is correct: Airy's isostatic model holds that crustal blocks of uniform density float at heights proportional to their thickness. A mountain, being a thick crustal block, must have a deeper root (below Moho) to displace enough mantle material and achieve gravitational equilibrium — exactly like an iceberg floating in water where the draft (submerged portion) is proportional to height above the surface.

Causal linkage: R directly and correctly explains A. The principle of isostasy (R) is the physical reason why the Moho is deeper under mountains (A). The correct answer is (a).

Value Addition:
• The isostatic root under the Himalayas extends to ~70 km — the deepest Moho on the Indian subcontinent.
• Post-orogenic erosion gradually reduces mountain mass → Moho rises → isostatic rebound elevates surface again (erosion-uplift cycle).
• GPS measurements now directly confirm isostatic uplift rates in eroded ancient mountain ranges like the Appalachians.

solution.concept_anchor: Mantle convection engine of plate tectonics; slab pull dominant mechanism
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) pairs 'Ridge push' with 'primary driver of plate tectonics' — students who remember ridge push as a named mechanism may accept it as the primary driver without knowing slab pull is more dominant.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — ridge push is a real mechanism (spreading ridges push plates outward) but is not the most dominant driver; slab pull is currently considered more significant.

Eliminate option (b) — mantle plumes (hot spots) are stationary heat sources and create island chains as plates move over them; attributing plate tectonics' driving force to mantle plumes alone is incorrect — they are localised phenomena.

Evaluate option (c) — radioactive decay of isotopes (U-238, Th-232, K-40) in Earth's crust and mantle contributing to the heat that drives mantle convection is a correctly matched pair; this is factually accurate.

Eliminate option (d) — the geodynamo in the outer core generates Earth's magnetic field, not the energy that drives plate motion; conflating magnetic field generation with plate tectonic driving force is an entity-swap error.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is a conflation trap — ridge push is a legitimate mechanism of plate tectonics, so students accept it as the 'primary driver.' The key distinction is that while ridge push exists and contributes, slab pull (not listed as an option) is more dominant, and mantle convection (fuelled by radioactive and primordial heat) is the overarching engine. Option (a) both misidentifies the mechanism and overrates its dominance. Option (c) correctly pairs radiogenic heat with mantle convection — a factually sound and precisely described relationship.
solution.final_explanation:
The driving forces of plate tectonics are rooted in Earth's internal heat — distinguishing which mechanism plays which role is critical.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched. Ridge push contributes to plate motion but is NOT the primary driver. Current geophysical consensus holds slab pull (gravitational sinking of dense subducting slabs) as more dominant than ridge push.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. Mantle plumes (hot spots) are stationary, localised heat anomalies that create volcanic features like Hawaii or the Deccan Traps. They are not the primary driver of global plate motion, which is mantle convection.
• Option (c): Correctly matched. Radioactive decay of U-238, U-235, Th-232 and K-40 in the crust and mantle generates radiogenic heat, which — combined with primordial heat — sustains mantle convection. This convection is the fundamental engine of plate tectonics.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. The geodynamo operates in the liquid outer core and generates Earth's magnetic field — it does not drive plate movement. Conflating magnetic field generation with tectonic driving force is a category error.

Value Addition:
• Earth loses ~47 TW of heat globally; roughly half is radiogenic, half primordial.
• Slab pull is evidenced by faster-moving plates (Pacific) having larger subduction zones than slower plates (African).
• Radioactive heating decreases over geological time — Earth's tectonic intensity billions of years ago was far greater.

solution.concept_anchor: Surface waves slower than body waves; Love vs Rayleigh wave distinction

statement_analysis.statement: Love waves are a type of surface wave that move the ground in a horizontal, side-to-side motion perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
statement_analysis.reason: Love waves (named after A.E.H. Love) are surface waves that generate horizontal shear motion — the ground moves from side to side perpendicular to the wave's travel direction, making them particularly damaging to building foundations.

statement_analysis.statement: Rayleigh waves travel faster than both P-waves and S-waves and are therefore the first seismic waves recorded on a seismograph after an earthquake.
statement_analysis.reason: Rayleigh waves are surface waves and are the slowest of all seismic waves — they arrive last at a seismograph, not first. P-waves are the fastest and arrive first, followed by S-waves, and then surface waves including Rayleigh waves.

statement_analysis.statement: Despite being the slowest seismic waves, surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) cause the greatest destruction during earthquakes because they have the largest amplitude and travel along Earth's surface where human settlements are located.
statement_analysis.reason: Surface waves have the lowest velocity but the highest amplitude of ground motion; since they travel along the surface, they interact directly with buildings and infrastructure, causing the most structural damage in earthquakes.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' tempts students who assume that 'surface waves cause most destruction' (Statement 3) must logically mean they are fastest — accepting Statement 2 as corroborating this assumption.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2 — Rayleigh waves are surface waves and are the slowest seismic waves; P-waves arrive first; the claim that Rayleigh waves 'travel faster than P-waves and S-waves' is fundamentally incorrect; Statement 2 is wrong.
Evaluate Statement 1 — Love waves producing horizontal side-to-side ground motion perpendicular to propagation is the textbook definition; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — surface waves causing most destruction due to large amplitude and surface travel path is a standard seismological fact; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a reversed-temporal trap combined with a scope-extension error. Students know surface waves are 'important' and 'powerful' and may conflate destructive power with speed — leading them to accept the false claim that Rayleigh waves are fastest. In fact, the arrival sequence on a seismograph is: P-waves (fastest) → S-waves → Surface waves (slowest). Surface waves are most destructive not because of speed but because of amplitude and their interaction with surface structures.
solution.final_explanation:
Seismic waves are classified into body waves (P and S) that travel through Earth's interior and surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) that travel along Earth's surface.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Love waves produce horizontal transverse ground motion — side-to-side shaking perpendicular to the wave direction. They cannot travel through water and are the most damaging to structures with shallow foundations.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Rayleigh waves are surface waves and are the slowest seismic waves — they arrive at seismographs last, after P-waves and S-waves. P-waves are fastest (~6–8 km/s in crust), S-waves are next (~3.5–4.5 km/s), and surface waves are slowest (~2–4 km/s).
• Statement 3 — Correct: Despite being slowest, surface waves carry the highest energy amplitude at the surface and cause the most structural damage. Their elliptical (Rayleigh) or lateral (Love) ground motion is most hazardous to buildings, bridges and pipelines.

Value Addition:
• Seismographs record the sequence: P-wave arrival → S-wave arrival → surface wave arrival (low-frequency, high-amplitude).
• Rayleigh waves produce an elliptical rolling motion — similar to ocean surface waves — both vertical and horizontal.
• The time gap between P and S wave arrivals at a seismograph is used to calculate the distance to the earthquake epicentre.

solution.concept_anchor: Geodynamo in liquid outer core; polarity reversals over thousands of years not suddenly

statement_analysis.statement: Convective motion within the solid inner core generates the electromagnetic currents responsible for Earth's geodynamo and magnetic field.
statement_analysis.reason: Earth's magnetic field is generated in the LIQUID outer core, not the solid inner core. The solid inner core cannot sustain convective currents. The geodynamo requires liquid, electrically conducting fluid in motion — a property of the outer core only.

statement_analysis.statement: Magnetic polarity reversals, in which the magnetic north and south poles exchange positions, occur suddenly over periods of a few decades.
statement_analysis.reason: Polarity reversals occur gradually over thousands to tens of thousands of years, not decades. During the transition, the magnetic field weakens before re-establishing in the opposite orientation.

statement_analysis.statement: The symmetric pattern of alternating normal and reversed magnetic polarity stripes on either side of mid-ocean ridges provided crucial evidence for the theory of seafloor spreading.
statement_analysis.reason: As new oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges, iron minerals crystallise in alignment with the prevailing magnetic field. Successive reversals produce symmetric magnetic striping that matched the predicted pattern of seafloor spreading — a key confirmation of plate tectonic theory.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) '2 only' tempts students who know polarity reversals don't happen suddenly (correctly rejecting Statement 2) but wrongly accept Statement 1 about the inner core generating the geodynamo — the entity-swap trap.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — the geodynamo operates in the LIQUID outer core, not the solid inner core; solid material cannot sustain convective currents needed for electromagnetic generation; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — polarity reversals take thousands to tens of thousands of years, not a few decades; the 'sudden' qualifier makes it NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — magnetic striping at mid-ocean ridges as evidence for seafloor spreading is a factual cornerstone of plate tectonic theory; Statement 3 is correct and must NOT be selected.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the entity-swap between the outer and inner core. Both are iron-nickel, and students who associate 'magnetic field = iron core' without specifying which layer will accept Statement 1. The critical distinction is that only the LIQUID outer core can sustain the convective fluid motion necessary for electromagnetic induction. Statement 2 exploits the misconception that polarity reversals are catastrophic sudden events — in reality, they are geologically gradual processes spanning thousands of years.
solution.final_explanation:
Earth's magnetic field and its reversals are products of the liquid outer core's geodynamo — precise attribution to the correct layer is essential.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The geodynamo operates exclusively in the LIQUID outer core (~2,900–5,100 km). Liquid iron-nickel in convective motion generates electric currents through electromagnetic induction. The solid inner core cannot sustain convective motion and plays no role in generating the magnetic field.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Polarity reversals are gradual geological processes spanning thousands to tens of thousands of years. The most recent reversal (Brunhes-Matuyama, ~780,000 years ago) unfolded over an extended period during which the field weakened significantly before re-establishing in the reversed direction.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis (1963) used the symmetric magnetic striping to confirm seafloor spreading — this was one of the most important pieces of evidence that established plate tectonic theory.

Value Addition:
• During polarity transition, the magnetosphere weakens to ~10% of normal — increasing cosmic ray exposure.
• Earth has undergone ~170 polarity reversals in the past 76 million years — average interval ~450,000 years.
• The inner core may have its own magnetic field signature due to its crystalline iron structure — an active area of research.

solution.concept_anchor: Deccan Traps formation timing and mantle plume origin
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places Deccan Traps formation after the K-Pg boundary, tempting students who know they are 'associated with' the extinction event but wrongly place them as a consequence rather than a near-simultaneous event straddling the boundary.
elimination_logic: Anchor the earliest event — Hawaiian island chain formation began millions of years ago as the Pacific plate moved over a stationary mantle plume; the oldest islands are oldest in the sequence.
Identify Deccan Traps timing — the Deccan Traps erupted primarily ~66 million years ago, straddling the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary; they began slightly before the K-Pg event.
Identify most recent polarity reversal — the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal occurred ~780,000 years ago — far more recent than Deccan Traps.

Identify Kola Superdeep Borehole — this was drilled 1970–1992 CE — the most recent event; correct order: Hawaiian chain initiation → Deccan Traps → Brunhes-Matuyama reversal → Kola Borehole; select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the placement of the Deccan Traps relative to the K-Pg boundary. Students who know the Deccan Traps are 'associated with' the extinction event may place them after it — as if volcanic activity was a consequence of the asteroid impact. In fact, the Deccan Traps began erupting slightly before the K-Pg boundary (~66.5–66 Ma) and continued after it. The chronological ordering within geological events requires precision about 'before the extinction' versus 'after the extinction.'
solution.final_explanation:
Geological events related to Earth's interior span a vast timescale from millions of years ago to recent scientific endeavours.

Correct chronological order:

1. Hawaiian island chain initiation (~70–80 million years ago): The Pacific plate began moving over the stationary Hawaiian mantle plume, forming the Emperor Seamount chain first, then the Hawaiian chain — oldest islands farthest from active Kilauea.

2. Deccan Traps formation (~66 million years ago): A massive mantle plume (now located under Réunion Island) triggered flood basalt eruptions in peninsular India, straddling the K-Pg boundary.

3. Brunhes-Matuyama magnetic polarity reversal (~780,000 years ago): The most recent full polarity reversal, recorded in seafloor sediments globally — far more recent than the Deccan Traps.

4. Kola Superdeep Borehole drilling (1970–1992 CE): The Soviet attempt to drill Earth's crust, reaching 12.2 km — the deepest direct penetration of Earth's interior.

Value Addition:
• The Deccan Traps cover ~500,000 km² of the Deccan Plateau — one of the largest volcanic provinces on Earth.
• Some scientists argue Deccan volcanism contributed more to the K-Pg extinction than the Chicxulub impact — a debated hypothesis.
• The Hawaiian mantle plume is estimated to originate ~2,000–2,700 km deep — possibly near the core-mantle boundary.

solution.concept_anchor: Meteorite analogy as corroborating evidence for core composition
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'deep-ocean drilling penetrating the mantle' sounds like plausible scientific evidence but no such penetration has occurred; students unfamiliar with the limits of drilling technology may accept it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — volcanic eruptions bring magma from the asthenosphere/lower crust to the surface, not from the core; lava composition reflects mantle/crust sources, not core composition.
Eliminate option (c) — no drilling has penetrated the mantle; the deepest borehole reached ~12.2 km (Kola), far short of the Moho even under oceans; this is a plausible fabrication.
Eliminate option (d) — gravitational measurements provide indirect evidence about mass distribution but cannot identify specific minerals or chemical composition of the core.

Confirm option (b) — iron meteorites (siderites) are compositionally analogous to Earth's core (iron-nickel); stony meteorites correspond to the mantle/crust. This meteorite analogy is one of the key supporting evidences for inferring core composition.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) is a plausible-fabrication trap. Deep-sea drilling programs (DSDP, ODP, IODP) are real and students know about them. The fabrication is that they have 'penetrated the mantle' — this has never occurred. The shallowest Moho is ~5–7 km under thin oceanic crust, and even this has never been drilled through. Students who equate 'deep-sea drilling' with 'deep into Earth' fall for this option. The correct answer (b) — meteorite analogy — is a less-taught but standard evidence used in earth science.
solution.final_explanation:
Establishing Earth's core composition requires indirect methods since no direct sampling is possible below ~12 km.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Volcanic lavas originate in the asthenosphere or lower crust — not the core. Lava analysis informs mantle composition, not core composition.
• Option (b): Correct. Iron meteorites (siderites) and stony-iron meteorites are compositionally similar to what Earth's core is inferred to contain — iron-nickel alloy. Since meteorites are remnants of early solar system differentiation (analogous to Earth's formation process), their composition serves as a chemical analogue for Earth's layers: iron meteorites ↔ core; stony meteorites ↔ mantle/crust.
• Option (c): Incorrect. No drilling program has penetrated the mantle. Deep-sea drilling programs sample oceanic sediments and upper oceanic crust. Project Mohole (1960s) attempted mantle penetration but was abandoned. This is a plausible fabrication designed to exploit students' familiarity with drilling programs.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Gravitational measurements (moment of inertia, gravity anomalies) reveal mass distribution within Earth but cannot identify specific chemical composition of the core.

Value Addition:
• Moment of inertia factor: ~0.33 for Earth (uniform sphere = 0.4) — proves mass concentrated toward centre.
• Seismology remains the most comprehensive evidence; meteorite analogy is the best compositional corroboration.
• Pallasite meteorites (olivine crystals in iron-nickel matrix) may represent ancient core-mantle boundary material from differentiated asteroids.

solution.concept_anchor: Convection currents in mantle driven by radioactive and primordial heat
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'slab pull alone' is a strong distractor because slab pull is the dominant single mechanism at subduction zones, and students may select it without recognising that the scenario specifically asks about what drives convection currents in the mantle — a broader phenomenon than slab pull.
elimination_logic: Identify the scenario's key question — what drives convective circulation in the mantle that in turn moves the tectonic plates; this is asking about the energy source and mechanism of mantle convection.
Eliminate option (b) — Earth's rotation (Coriolis effect) influences atmospheric and oceanic circulation but is not a recognised driver of mantle convection or plate tectonics.

Eliminate option (c) — slab pull is the result of dense, cold slabs sinking at subduction zones; it drives plate movement at those specific zones but does not explain the broader mantle convection engine or why convection exists in the first place.

Eliminate option (d) — geodynamo currents in the outer core generate the magnetic field but do not drive mantle convection or plate movement; select option (a) — heat from radioactive decay in the mantle/crust and primordial heat from accretion together fuel mantle convection, which is the primary engine.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) is the reversed-causation trap. Slab pull is a consequence/mechanism of plate tectonics at subduction zones — it is driven by the density of the sinking slab, which itself formed through mantle convection and crustal differentiation. The question asks what drives the convection that moves plates broadly — the answer is the heat sources (radioactive decay + primordial heat), not slab pull, which is a secondary mechanism within an already-moving system.
solution.final_explanation:
Mantle convection is the fundamental engine of plate tectonics — and its energy source is a combination of heat from two distinct origins.

The scenario describes scientists observing slow (~2–10 cm/year) horizontal movement of continents and seeking the root cause of the mantle's convective circulation. This requires identifying the energy source, not just the mechanisms.

• Option (a): Correct. Two heat sources drive mantle convection: (i) primordial heat — retained from Earth's formation by gravitational compression and early differentiation (~4.5 billion years ago); (ii) radiogenic heat — ongoing radioactive decay of U-238, Th-232 and K-40 in crust and mantle. The thermal gradient drives hot mantle material upward and cooler material downward — generating convection cells that move plates.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Earth's rotation generates the Coriolis effect in fluids (atmosphere, ocean) but does not drive mantle convection. The mantle's viscosity is too high for rotational effects to dominate.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Slab pull is a mechanism of plate movement at subduction zones — not the energy source of mantle convection. It is a consequence of the convective system, not its cause.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The geodynamo in the outer core generates the magnetic field. It does not transmit energy to drive mantle convection or plate motion.

Value Addition:
• Heat flow from Earth's interior: ~47 terawatts total — roughly split between primordial and radiogenic sources.
• Mantle convection cells are not simple loops — seismic tomography reveals complex 3D patterns of upwelling and downwelling.
• Ridge push contributes ~5–10% of the energy driving plate motion; slab pull contributes ~90%.

solution.concept_anchor: Moho is compositional not temperature boundary; Gutenberg most diagnostic

statement_analysis.statement: The Mohorovičić Discontinuity is primarily a temperature boundary where the geothermal gradient undergoes a sharp change, transitioning from the cooler crust to the hotter mantle.
statement_analysis.reason: The Moho is a compositional and seismic velocity boundary — P-wave speed increases suddenly from ~6–7 km/s (crust) to ~8 km/s (mantle). Temperature changes gradually across the Moho; it is not a temperature boundary.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gutenberg Discontinuity at ~2,900 km is more seismically diagnostic than the Moho for understanding the physical state of Earth's core, because it is where S-waves are completely blocked.
statement_analysis.reason: The Gutenberg Discontinuity marks the mantle–outer core boundary and is where S-waves stop entirely, proving the outer core is liquid — the most fundamental inference about core state. This makes it more diagnostically significant than the Moho for understanding core properties.

statement_analysis.statement: The Lehmann Discontinuity separates the crust from the upper mantle and was discovered by analysing the sudden increase in P-wave velocity at approximately 35 km depth.
statement_analysis.reason: The Lehmann Discontinuity separates the outer core from the inner core at ~5,100 km depth — not the crust from the mantle. The crust-mantle boundary is the Moho. Inge Lehmann discovered it by detecting P-waves within the expected S-wave shadow zone, not at 35 km depth.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) '2 only' is close to the correct answer (c) but leads students who misread and think Statement 2 is also incorrect — students who are unsure whether Gutenberg is truly 'more diagnostic than Moho' may reject Statement 2 as well.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Moho as a 'temperature boundary' is factually incorrect; it is defined by seismic velocity change and compositional difference, not temperature; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Gutenberg Discontinuity being more seismically diagnostic than Moho for core state inference (via S-wave blockage) is correct; Statement 2 is correct and must NOT be selected.

Evaluate Statement 3 — Lehmann Discontinuity at 35 km separating crust from mantle is a compound error: Lehmann is at ~5,100 km (outer-inner core boundary), not 35 km; the 35 km boundary is the Moho; Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a double entity-swap trap: it assigns the Lehmann Discontinuity's function (outer-inner core boundary) to the Moho's depth (35 km) and simultaneously attributes the Moho's function (crust-mantle boundary at 35 km) to the Lehmann Discontinuity's name. Students who have partially memorised discontinuity names without their specific depths and functions are highly susceptible to this compound confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
Precise knowledge of each discontinuity's nature, depth, discoverer and diagnostic significance is essential to avoid the entity-swap traps prevalent in UPSC.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Moho is NOT a temperature boundary. Temperature increases gradually across the Moho — no sharp temperature discontinuity exists. The Moho is defined by a sudden jump in seismic wave velocity (P-waves from ~6–7 to ~8 km/s) and a compositional change from felsic/mafic crust to ultramafic mantle.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Gutenberg Discontinuity (~2,900 km) is the most seismically diagnostic boundary for inferring core state — it is where S-waves stop entirely, proving the outer core is liquid. The Moho reveals the crust-mantle boundary but does not tell us about core state.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This statement contains two errors. First, the Lehmann Discontinuity is at ~5,100 km (outer core–inner core boundary), not 35 km. Second, the boundary at ~35 km separating crust from mantle is the Moho, not the Lehmann Discontinuity. Inge Lehmann discovered the inner core in 1936 by detecting P-waves within the shadow zone.

Value Addition:
• Moho = seismic velocity boundary; Gutenberg = S-wave cessation boundary; Lehmann = P-wave velocity increase boundary (solid inner core).
• The Moho was named after Andrija Mohorovičić (Croatian seismologist, 1909 discovery).
• Gutenberg also calculated the size of the liquid outer core to within a few kilometres of modern estimates — a remarkable achievement using 1910s seismographs.

solution.concept_anchor: Physical state of each Earth layer correctly matched

statement_analysis.statement: Continental crust — solid, granitic composition, density ~2.7 g/cm³, thickness ~35–70 km
statement_analysis.reason: Continental crust is solid, composed predominantly of granite (SIAL — Silica + Aluminium), with density ~2.7 g/cm³ and thickness ranging from ~35 km under plains to ~70 km under mountain ranges — all standard facts.

statement_analysis.statement: Asthenosphere — liquid layer within the upper mantle, source of all magma, depth ~100–200 km
statement_analysis.reason: The asthenosphere is NOT liquid — it is a solid that behaves plastically over geological timescales with ~1–5% partial melt. It is also not the source of 'all' magma — magma originates from various depths including the lower crust.

statement_analysis.statement: Outer core — liquid iron-nickel alloy, depth ~2,900–5,100 km, responsible for Earth's magnetic field via geodynamo
statement_analysis.reason: The outer core is confirmed liquid (S-wave blockage evidence), composed of iron-nickel, and is the site of the geodynamo — all three attributes are correct and precisely stated.

statement_analysis.statement: Inner core — solid iron-nickel, depth ~5,100–6,371 km, solid due to lowest temperatures in Earth's interior
statement_analysis.reason: The inner core is solid NOT because of low temperatures — it is the hottest region (~5,000–6,000°C). It is solid because the immense pressure (~330–360 GPa) raises the melting point of iron-nickel above the ambient temperature.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify Statement 2 as wrong (asthenosphere not liquid) but wrongly accept Statement 4 (inner core solid because coolest) — a common misconception.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2 — 'liquid layer' for asthenosphere is incorrect (it is plastic/ductile solid); 'all magma' is a scope-extension error; Statement 2 is incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 4 — inner core described as solid due to 'lowest temperatures' is fundamentally wrong; inner core has the highest temperatures but is solidified by pressure; Statement 4 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 1 — continental crust as solid, granitic, ~2.7 g/cm³, ~35–70 km thick — all accurate; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — outer core as liquid iron-nickel at 2,900–5,100 km responsible for geodynamo — all accurate; Statement 3 is correct. Only two are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 targets the most persistent misconception about the inner core: students assume 'solid = cold' and 'liquid = hot.' This is intuitive from everyday experience but wrong under extreme pressure. The inner core is ~5,000–6,000°C — among the hottest regions on Earth — but pressure (~330 GPa) forces it into solid state. Statement 2 targets the equally common 'asthenosphere = liquid lava layer' misconception. Together, both wrong statements are designed to be accepted by students who have only superficial knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The physical states of Earth's layers are non-intuitive because pressure effects dominate over temperature at great depth.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Continental crust is solid, granitic (SIAL), ~2.7 g/cm³, 35–70 km thick.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The asthenosphere is NOT liquid — it is solid with ~1–5% partial melt, making it ductile/plastic. Calling it 'liquid' and the source of 'all' magma are both errors.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Outer core is liquid iron-nickel at ~2,900–5,100 km depth, responsible for geodynamo — all three attributes correctly stated.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The inner core is solid NOT due to low temperatures. It is the hottest part of Earth (~5,000–6,000°C). Solidification is due to extreme confining pressure (~330 GPa) raising the iron-nickel melting point above ambient temperature.

Correct physical state sequence: Solid crust → Plastic asthenosphere → Solid lower mantle → Liquid outer core → Solid inner core.

Value Addition:
• The boundary between the plastic asthenosphere and rigid lithosphere (LAB) is the most tectono-geologically significant internal boundary for surface processes.
• Pressure-driven solidification is the Clausius-Clapeyron effect applied to iron-nickel at core conditions.
• Seismic evidence for inner core solidity: P-waves passing through the inner core (PKIKP waves) arrive slightly earlier than expected — consistent with higher velocity in solid material.

solution.concept_anchor: Airy vs Pratt isostasy model distinction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Pratt's model' is the strong distractor because both Airy and Pratt models explain isostasy, and students who remember 'Pratt involves density' may confuse which model uses density variation versus thickness variation.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — the Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis explains magnetic striping at mid-ocean ridges as evidence for seafloor spreading; it is unrelated to isostasy models.

Evaluate option (b) — Pratt's model explains isostasy through varying density with uniform crustal base depth; 'mountains composed of less dense material' aligns with Pratt, not Airy; but the blank specifically asks about the 'deeper root' mechanism which is Airy.
Eliminate option (c) — the Carey hypothesis relates to continental drift through Earth expansion; not an isostasy model.

Confirm option (d) — Airy's model proposes that crustal blocks of uniform density but varying thickness (mountains have deeper roots like icebergs) achieve isostatic equilibrium; the 'deeper root' mechanism is the defining feature of Airy's model.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (b) and (d) are designed to exploit the Airy-Pratt confusion. The key distinguishing feature: Airy's model — same density, different thickness (deeper roots under mountains). Pratt's model — same base depth, different density (mountains are less dense). The blank emphasises 'deeper crustal root' which is unambiguously Airy's model. Students who have memorised 'isostasy has two models' without distinguishing the mechanism of each will select Pratt's model as an equally valid answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Isostasy has two competing models that explain how elevated terrain achieves gravitational equilibrium with the underlying mantle.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis explains the symmetric magnetic striping on the seafloor as evidence of seafloor spreading — entirely unrelated to the isostasy question.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Pratt's model attributes mountain height to density variation — mountains are less dense than adjacent lowlands, with all crustal blocks reaching the same depth (compensation depth). The 'deeper root' mechanism belongs to Airy, not Pratt.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Carey hypothesis relates to an expanding Earth theory as an alternative to plate tectonics — not an isostasy model.
• Option (d): Correct. Airy's model proposes that all crustal blocks have the same density but different thicknesses. Mountains are like icebergs — the portion above sea level (surface topography) is supported by a proportionally deep crustal root below the Moho. Higher mountains = deeper roots.

Value Addition:
• Memory aid: A = Airy = Above and below (same density, different depth); P = Pratt = Properties vary (density varies, base is level).
• The Himalayan crustal root (~70 km Moho depth) perfectly demonstrates Airy's isostasy.
• In reality, both mechanisms operate — real mountain systems exhibit elements of both Airy and Pratt isostasy.
